text_full: It Does NOT Work for me. When I opened the box containing the Verilux Original Floor Lamp I knew I had my perfect light computer workstation light. The height and availability of a flexible light head were just perfect. The color of the fixture fit well. The light itself has two levels of brightness and each is controlled by a toggle switch in a perfect location under the head. A flexible next permits ease of setup and ease of changing just the head's position. The base is heavy enough to keep the unbalanced head from tilting over during most operations and I have yet to find a position that would cause it to fall over. Then constructing the lamp from 3 pieces plus 2 1/4 inch screws (critical to construction) turned into a semi-nightmare. The internal cord was so stiff it took major tinkering. It is just a bit too long and it needs to be near perfect to make for the ideal connection between the base and the extension rod going to the head. After I finally connnected the base to the extension with one of the screws I found that the screw was just too small to hold the assembly above the base. I held the extension in place, connected the head with the other screw and found a similar but not quite as bad connection. Finally, I plugged the cord into the outlet and the light at either level is nice and handy. I took a "gather my wits" break and returned a few moments later to move the light to its permanent place. I forgot about the screw and just lifted the light by the extension and the bottom fell off. Oops and it never worked as it was intended to work. I refused to be outdone by a lamp and make my very own Rube Goldberg light at my work station in the garage by plugging the cord into an outlet and attaching the base's cord to the head without the extension. I placed the head above the area that I use for close and tedious work such as fixing watches, clocks or computer parts and am happy with the results. Even though the original setup is faulty the final product is at least useful. Maybe I should have considered a higher score but it was too much work for such an outcome.

While not a deal-breaker, this means you have to hold on to your sleeves while you pull the jacket on so they don't bunch up. Finally, it's partially my fault for not reading more carefully, but this jacket came up when I searched Amazon for "waterproof ski jacket" - so I assumed at least it would be waterproof. Alas, per the description, it's only 'water resistant' - and honestly that's a stretch. Indeed, when I ran it under the tap it got wet (see image). To be fair, the water beaded a little at first, but don't expect this to keep you dry for long. I'm giving it 3 stars because I suppose it's a decent windbreaker, it has a nice zipper, and the pockets are nice, but I'm going to have to order another jacket for my ski trip. Would not recommend unless you're slim/athletic and you're only using it for 'around the town' on chilly (but not frigid) days.

text_full: Great looking "bracelet" ... but look elsewhere if you want an actual watch.. Automatic mechanical watches have never been my cup of tea, but this one kept popping up in online ads and catching my attention. At $100 for a Chinese fashion watch, my interest stopped at window shopping, but when I saw it on Amazon for a lot less than that, and then realized I could shave a few more bucks off the price with some reward points, I decided to give it a try. The watch comes securely packed in a neat, black Lige box with a fold-over, magnetic lid, and small instruction booklet, cleaning cloth, warranty card, and a little tool you can use for pushing the two hidden buttons on opposite sides of the crown. Features and Functions ... The watch is equipped with hour/minute hands only (no second hand), and 3 sub-dials: day-of-week; calendar day, and 24-hour dial with underlying sun/moon/a.m./p.m. disc. The day-of-week and calendar day dials are adjusted by two hidden pushbuttons on opposite sides of the crown. One push = one unit on the corresponding dial. In normal operation, or when you’re adjusting the watch for the first time, don’t get thrown if both sub-dials don’t advance at midnight. The calendar-day sub-dial advances at midnight. The day-of-week subdial advances between 1:30 and 2:30 a.m. The 24-hour dial revolves once every 24 hours. The sun/moon disc beneath the dial is NOT a moon phase indicator ... just an am/pm indicator. It’s literally mounted on the same post as the dial hand. The sub-dials and numbers/alpha characters on them are nicely designed, but really tiny, so if your vision isn’t so hot, you won't have much fun trying to see/use them. The crystal isn’t flat, but a little convex, so it neatly compliments the rounded edges of the gold bezel surrounding it, and has a magnifying glass effect as you turn the watch sideways. The finish color on the body isn’t quite rose gold, and not quite yellow, but somewhere in between. I like it ... gives the watch an antique patina look. The main hands are the same color as the watch body. This watch is pretty “chunky” (I used a caliper to measure it: 15mm from crystal to back, 43mm in diameter). The diameter is fine ... the thickness, not so much. Even my divers watch is thinner. It’s supposedly water resistant to 5 atmospheres (or, 50 meters/164 feet), but I wouldn’t trust this thing in water, at any depth or length of time. I’m guessing it’s far more vulnerable to water intrusion/damage than 5 atmospheres, e.g., at the crown opening. It’ll probably survive splashes and brief, shallow immersions, but get it out and dry it off promptly, and don’t press your luck. In the face opening below the main hands, there’s a little adjustment lever and bar graph below it, marked from 0 to 20 in increments of 5. This lever isn’t accessible without opening the watch case ... probably there for use by service techs (or adventurous DIY’ers) to adjust the speed of the watch, if necessary. However, after 24 hours of careful comparison of the movement to the clock on my computer, the factory setting kept perfect time ... WHEN IT WAS RUNNING. More on that below. The see-through back reveals a brass-colored auto-wind counterweight, which contrasts nicely with the stainless steel "guts" underneath it. The parts under the counterweight are all machined with attractive, linear patterns that greatly enhance the look of the see-through back. About the band and clasp ... The band that comes with the watch is supposedly leather ... dark brown, embossed with a croc pattern on the outside, and smooth gray leather on the inside. Honestly, I can’t tell if it’s genuine leather or not. If not, it’s a darn good fake ... sturdy, pliable ... a decent, attractive band for the price. The band is fitted with a clasp that combines typical hole adjustment with the sort of folding clasp normally used on bracelet watches. Interesting, but I think I would have preferred a traditional buckle, mainly because I had a heck of a time figuring out how to work this thing. No explanation of how this particular clasp works in the instructions. It's actually pretty easy once you figure it out, though: select the hole/length that’s best for your wrist, and secure a separate clasp on that, then little spring-loaded buttons on opposite sides of the main clasp unlock/open up both ends of the band, more than wide enough to get the watch on/off your hand without having to mess with the hole clasp again. I guess that's the main benefit of this kind of clasp ... eliminates the wear/tear of taking a buckle on/off the leather every time, and greatly extends the service life of the band. Best thing for me, I have a large-ish wrist (about 8 inches around), and the band/clasp actually fit me comfortably with the adjustment set on the second-to-last hole. The lug width of the band is 22mm (I measured it with a caliper, so trust me ... not the sales copy), so should be easy to find a replacement, if necessary. About “automatic” mechanical watches ... This stuff may seem obvious to all us old-timers, but for all you kids out there who’ve been weaned on battery-powered everything, mechanical watches don’t run on electricity from a battery. They’re powered by tension stored in a coiled mainspring. When the spring tension is fully released, the watch stops, and the spring has to be manually re-wound/tightened to restart the watch. An automatic watch winds the mainspring via an internal counterweight that spins with normal movement of your arm/body while you’re wearing it. Thus, a properly functioning automatic watch should never have to be manually wound as long as you’re wearing it, and you’re reasonably active. However, that also means if you want the watch to run continuously without having to be reset or manually wound, you have to wear it pretty much every day. The implications for anyone who keeps/wears a number of different watches should be obvious ... you’re going to be re-starting/re-setting your automatic watch a lot. A reminder that China is not Switzerland ... Now, all the little gears and gizmos in a mechanical watch are pretty delicate, and all of them need to be made of the highest quality metals, and fit and work together very precisely for the watch to run normally and keep decent time. This is even more important in an automatic watch. All the problems traditionally associated with overwinding of the mainspring (e.g., breakage, movement getting stuck, etc.) are supposed to be controlled by a thing called a bridle, or, a kind of clutch that disables both auto and manual winding functions when the mainspring has reached maximum tension. For some reason I never figured out, the watch I received kept stopping for no apparent reason, no matter how much I wound it, shook it to restart it, and/or tried to purposely spin the auto-winder. The problem is made worse by the fact that the manual winding mechanism on this watch is very quiet and low-resistance, e.g., hard/impossible to know when the mainspring is fully wound. In the end, this purchase reminded me why battery-powered quartz watches basically wiped out all makers of budget mechanical watches, and I ended up returning it to Amazon for a refund. Conclusion ... That’s the difference between a Chinese-made, automatic mechanical watch that costs less than a hundred bucks, and a German, Swiss or other, more-reputable equivalent that costs $500 (or more). The closer you look at the former, the less you like it. The closer you look at the latter, the more you like it, because you start to realize it cost what it did because the people who made it were life-long watchmakers who care more about their name/reputation, and the quality, function, reliability and longevity of the timepieces they make, than they care about making a quick buck off reverse-engineered, copy-cat junk, made from inferior materials that work just long enough to outlast the warranty (if you’re lucky), and are then forgotten and/or tossed in a landfill. For the record, this is the first time I can remember ever giving a one-star rating to any product I've purchased on Amazon, and that's a LOT of products over the years ... very surprised and disappointed.

text_full: They don't work, and they aren't as described. I can't believe I'm going to write such a long review about finger lights, but here goes... I've purchased finger lights before, and they were everything my kids hoped they'd be: they've had a very long life, the switch is easy to push, and the elastic is made of a comfortable black cloth. These are a whole different story. First, and most important, most of them didn't work properly. Out of 40 lights, 22 were useless: 6 didn't light up at all, 6 lit up so weakly that you couldn't even tell they were lit, and 10 could light up only if you held onto them and squeezed them hard in some elusive way (different for each one). Officially, the other 18 lights worked, but 11 of them had switches that were so difficult to operate that I didn't want to give them to a bunch of kids who would just find them frustrating. That left 7 good finger lights. Out of 40. I guess I can't expect more for something I paid less than $8 for. Aside from the fact that they don't work, they also don't match the description. First, the picture implies that they have a black cloth elastic. Nope. It's a rubbery colored elastic, which might be fine but looks like it'll split soon enough. I guess I'd be okay with this if the lights actually worked. Second, they are described as having an "easy push button." It is misleading to describe the on/off switch as a "button." And as I've already said, many of them are very hard to turn on, so "easy" is also a misnomer. Third, the description says you get "10 packs of 4 lights" and "each package will contain 4 finger lights each with a total of 10 packages you will receive." Nope. I received 40 lights all in a plastic bag, not 10 separate packs with the cardboard "hand" package pictured above. Again, not a big deal if the lights work! Last, the description also says you get "a total of 10 white finger lights, 10 blue finger lights, 10 red finger lights, and 10 green finger lights." I got 7 white lights, 10 blue lights, 10 red lights, and 13 green lights. Close, but another nope. This definitely wouldn't have been a problem for me--in fact, I probably wouldn't have even counted the colors--but since they don't work and I'm writing this review, I might as well be thorough! I don't know where to buy good finger lights, but these aren't them!

The T-980 is larger around and heavier than the older unit... enough so that I really miss the sense of control and precision I was used to. In short, the T-980 feels clumsier, less maneuverable, and less accurate. It takes longer to complete the job due to the hassle of changing the regular blade and the trimming blade. And it really tries my patience having to be so careful not to beak one of those delicate, sliding, plastic prongs or the vacuum-compartment cover. text_full: Not an eco-friendly company; would never purchase this product again.. States that their mission is to repurpose organic goods into innovative and eco-friendly products and that their packaging is 100% recyclable, and the exfoliating coffee grounds are repurposed to lower landfill waste. The bottom of the box reads: "Providing the highest quality beauty products while minimizing our footprint on the environment." First, the three soap bars you receive are little; like taking a normal sized bar of soap and cutting it three ways. As any soap user knows, once the bar is used down to a certain size, it's ready to be replaced. And since these pieces are already so small, it's not long before you reach the replacement decision point, but x 3, as opposed to x 1 for a normal sized bar of soap. So for a very high price for what's a normal sized bar of soap cut up three ways, you'll be going through these bars fast, possibly wasting more, and needing to buy more sooner -- not eco-friendly! The package is meant to give the impression of being earthy and eco-friendly. It's in a high-quality cardboard box (and not the recycled cardboard type), and the soap is surrounded with some shredded newspaper to give the impression of recycling/repurposing. Inside were some additional card inserts which were unnecessary. Then around Christmas time, I receive an enveloped Christmas Card (nice quality) from the “Urbanized Family" - at the time, I didn't know who the "Urbanized" family was or why they were sending me a card. Later I realized that the card was related to the soap purchase; - the card, of course, had gone right into the trash as junk mail. How very wasteful for a company touting itself as eco-friendly, wanting to help the world lower landfill waste, and promoting itself as a business with the goal of minimizing their “…footprint on the environment." In my opinion, overpriced soap (attractive looking and with a light scent, but nothing really special) and a marketing strategy insincerely meant to play to the conscious of people looking to spend their money in ways that contribute to a more eco-friendly world.

I am aware that you can purchase a case with the disc in it, but I do not want to as I paid a lot of money for this product. I feel that they might be ripping the consumer off by cutting back on the coating of the neutralizer. This might be that built in inflation control that you often see with products such as toilet paper companies shrinking their product. Either way, after my many years of using this product, I have decided to make the switch to a cleanser that uses tablets rather than a coated disc. I am fed up with burning eyes and being ripped off.

text_full: Pros and Cons to Consider. I have very dense, thick, and long 4C hair, so my texture is the most coarse texture of hair to possibly test the durability of this blower-dryer comb. Anyone that has coarse or thick hair such as yours truly, likely runs into the same problem as me when you blow dry your hair after a washing. The dang blow-dryer comb keeps popping off and/or the teeth bends and snaps off. So annoying! Since this is very expensive for a blow-dryer comb, I'm sure ladies will appreciate this critical review before purchasing. Here are the pros and cons I've come across. Pros...The material is the highest grade of plastic (not at all rubber) I have seen in a blow-dryer comb. It appears to be equivalent to the "plastic" material cooking utensils are made of, so the teeth does not easily bend/break. The finer and less dense your hair is, the longer the life-time you will have this comb. If you attach it securely, the comb actually works without popping off. Cons...This seems to only work for dryers with a narrow barrel, and not so much for the dryers that has a bubble shape. It will pop off dryers with a bubble shaped barrel, because it will be impossible to secure it on a nozzle tip that is not cylinder-shaped. All you need is a phillips screwdriver to attach it. Since I have 4C hair, I did actually notice slight bending of a couple teeth, and the bending increased after a 3rd usage. After my 3rd hair drying, I tried to hand-bend the teeth back in place, and 2 snapped off! $40 bucks (cost and shipping) down the drain :-( Also, what you don't know until you see it in person is that there is a metal bar inside the comb, that is being raked against your hair as you are combing it, which will eventually cause heat damage with prolonged usage, especially if you dry your hair on high. My overall assessment is that, yes it worked better that expected. Although 2 teeth broke on mine and others slightly bent, I plan on buying another one to have on-hand, as I currently have not come across any better options. But, I'm going to take a break from this comb for a while, and try drying my hair with a paddle brush and my dryer because the thought of that metal bar inside the Willie Morrow comb, raking against my hair with every usage is alarming, and will surely heat damage my hair.

text_full: Trendy Scarf (For Guys, Too!). I'm a guy that likes to dress nicely, and I figured I could use a scarf in the closet when it get cold here in Texas for two weeks out of the year. Considering what I paid for this scarf, I'm pleased. It's so thin though, you could pull a thread, then ruining it. Which leads to good and bad things. Bad: ruining means... ruining it. It'll be a rag for whatever then. It also means this isn't for really cold environments. Even in Texas cold for me, this barely does the warmth job outside. The Good? Since it's thin, it can be used in cooler temperatures or for style without making you sweat. So, for style, it's a good buy. For warmth, it's so-so. But with how cheap it is, having it destroyed by a snag will be less painful. Just watch out for thorns, zippers, and any other snaggable objects around you. January 18th, 2012 Update: Recently, I lost my scarf, so, knowing they were dirt cheap, I when't ahead and ordered another. It arrived within one week, but the smell of the scarf was atrocious. It reminded me of what a scarf that a dirty old man would were if he worked in the hot sun for long hours and showered in gasoline. It took a thorough hand wash, some cologne, and a few nights of wear to actually get the smell to become bearable. I fear for putting this in the wash as it might destroy the woven fabric. This experience dropped my score from a 4 star to a 3. I didn't call support to complain, but I believe this should be something that the company who sends these out should know about to begin with. If you buy these scarves and they smell awful, my best advise is to soak them in a sink, hang them to dry after spraying them with your favorite fragrance, and then toughing it out until it reaches the "your" scent. Just expect it to be an arduous task.

text_full: Not worth the hassle. At first I thought this was the greatest razor ever. It provides a smooth shave, probably the best shave I've ever encountered. I have very sensitive skin, so I have to be selective. First impressions: It is a very sleek and cool looking razor. It is so fancy, that I am afraid of breaking it every time I touch it. The problem with this razor is not its performance, rather it is the maintenance. The lotion is expensive, and to make things worse, it is nearly impossible to find, unless you are willing to spend lots of money and buy it online. But, the razor works, so I stuck it out. Next problem: Norelco suggests that you replace the cartridge for sanitary reasons each time you refill the lotion. OK, but when I ordered the lotion (which is supposed to come with the cartridge), THERE WAS NO CARTRIDGE! So, I decided to stick it out anyway. Each time I replaced the lotion, I would just remove the cartridge and clean it myself. That seemed fine, until this morning when I accidentally broke a piece of this fragile cartridge. Now, I can't get the lotion to come out, so the razor is ineffective. I tried to buy a new lotion with cartridge at Target, and the lotion came without the cartridge, so I have to return it. I know Phillips-Norelco has excellent customer service, so I called to see if they could help me. It turns out that the lotion does not always come with the cartridge (although it is advertised that way and I was told that it came with the cartridge by a customer service rep before I bought the razor). So, it's kind of like a little guessing game. Where can I find the lotion and cartridge together? Fun! I asked if they could just send me some cartridges, no lotion, just cartridges and I'd be happy. But they could not do that, so I am going to return this razor and get my money back. I still have a previous Norelco shaver (dry) and I will try that again, although it is not as good. I think in the end I may have to resort back to the painful manual razor shave. I have been a Norelco customer for many years and up to this point I was always very pleased, this is disappointing. To summarize: This is an excellent razor, but it is not worth the money or the hassle you have to go through to make it work effectively! I welcome any shaving advice to help my sensitive skin!

text_full: Nice...But Falls Short. If possible, I would have given this 2.5 stars. I like the design, but the materials used kind of ruin the anklet. It did arrive quickly, though. This is a pretty anklet. The silver chain is a bright silver beaded chain - it is very dainty and seems it would be very easy to break or kink. From my experience, that type of chain is sturdier than it appears, but it could be problematic to have it on an anklet. There are eight little decorative balls on each of the two chains, and the chains are fused together at the ends. Of the eight seamless balls, four are smooth and four are stardust sparkle, and all are about 3-4 mm. The two chains have alternated designs - one is stardust, smooth, stardust, smooth, etc. The other is smooth, stardust, smooth, stardust, etc. They go well with the bright silver chain. The balls are kept in place with silver crimp beads. It's a good way to keep the balls in the middle of the chains, but definitely not very a very sturdy method to use on an ankle bracelet. In this case, the crimp beads appear clumsy and ruin the flow of the design. All of that said, my biggest issue with this anklet is that it is WAY too small. It isn't even close to the stated length measurement of 25cm/9.84". Mine measures 21.1cm/8.3", 23cm/9" with the extension chain. At less than 2cm, I'm not real sure what is the point of the extension chain. Bottom Line: A beautiful anklet that will go with anything. It is about 4cm/1.57" shorter than advertised. It would fit much better as a large bracelet - due to the chain used in the design, it will not take much punishment before breaking, and this type of beaded chain is a difficult fix. The crimp beads are clumsy and will likely break with little wear. I like the design of the anklet, however, I think the chain is too dainty to last as an anklet...especially when the overall length is 1.57" shorter than the seller states. (And I was being a little generous with my measurements.) I would not buy this again - which is too bad. Had it been made with materials that are a little sturdier - and the RIGHT SIZE - this could have been an amazing little anklet that I would have worn daily. Designed as it is, there is no way this will stand up to daily abuse.

text_full: OK, but outperformed by a $10 foil electric. I got this shaver in early January of 2007. For the first month or so that I had it, it worked decently. The shave was relatively close and it did get most of the hair, but it did take a few passes over the skin, and a touch-up using the on-board trimmer to get the ones it missed. I also found myself having the stretch the skin quite a bit to get a close enough shave. However, it did offer an irritation-free shave (I have sensitive skin, thus why I stay away from blade razors). Over the next few months, though, I noticed that the shave started to get more irritating: more 'pulling' instead of cutting (had always pulled a little, but got more frequent), takes more passes to cut what it once would, etc. I changed the blades after 3 months (short period, yes, but I tried anyway). It helped a little, but it still wasn't as good as it once was. Then, I started to realize that the shaver wasn't holding as strong a charge as it once did. It would come off the charger and be 'full power' for less than one shave, and would need to go back on the charger after 6 shaves (far less than the advertised two weeks). A call to Norelco led nowhere, as they said it was 'expected' for the battery to wear down over time (4 months?). I kept using the razor as I wasn't about to waste the $90 investment. On a trip in late July, I had forgotten to pack the shaver, so I purchased a $10 Remington battery-operated foil razor at a local convenience store. Sad to say, but from Day 1 that foil razor has outperformed the Norelco by leaps and bounds in all areas (closer shave, gets all areas better, less passes needed, etc.). Also on a sad note, the Remington is kicking the bucket (a year later), and I am forced to go back to the Norelco for the time being while I look for an acceptable foil shaver as a replacement. In short, this razor performed decently at first, but it seems as though compared to a $10 battery operated razor, this $70 shaver isn't a good value for the investment.

text_full: Good taste, stays "clumpy". $$$. I ordered this product as it was listed as a "buy one, get one at half price" promotion, and it was created by the folks at Speed Keto, so I figured, sure, why not? Pros: Taste: I was looking for something other than chocolate, and this strawberry flavor is pretty good. it is very sweet tasting to me, although not overpowering. I like to add ice to it after blending and making an iced smoothie - yum! Ketosis: I don't have this every day but on days when I do, I have not noticed any problem remaining in ketosis as indicated by ketone measuring strips. It isn't designed to be a meal replacement although I have used this as a meal replacement on days when I have fallen out of ketosis to get back on track again. So, it works! Cons: Price: When I purchased the product, the cost was $44.95 for one (about $67.43 for 2, or $33.71 each on promo). The non-promo price has since dropped by $5.00 to $39.95 each. I think it's way overpriced, although one can argue that everything that says "keto" on it is too expensive. Blending Power: Not good at all! Even when I use a "Ninja Professional" mixer to try to dissolve all of the powder, I end up with too many clumps of dry powder within my drink, as compared to using Slim Fast's Keto powder in the same blender (which blends quite well, but really isn't all that keto friendly, but that's another story entirely). The Bottom Line: In spite of what I think of the price, and the subpar blending results, I still ordered another container of their product: the salted caramel flavor. Overall, the impact to staying in ketosis is a big plus in my book. I also realized that there are plenty of similarly marketed keto-shake powders available on Amazon.com which are just as expensive, if not more so (per serving), than this product. If the manufacturer could just work on the recipe so that the resulting drink isn't filled with so many undissolved powder balls, then I would likely rate this product four stars, if not higher.

text_full: Everything You Want to Know about Skincare Products. There are many things that unspecialized people must be aware of before purchasing and/or using any chemical or even herbal products. Anti aging cream products spread all over the market and many people are not aware of the ingredients, how they work, what are the qualities of a good anti aging cream product, and what are the side effects that such products may pose. You probably know the benefits of Vitamin C serum, but what about the hidden side of it? We know that vitamin C serum a) Acts as an antioxidant, b) Helps produce collagen, c) Restores skin damage. But the other side is often not highlighted from manufacturers. So, to unravel some of the mysteries about skin care products, I would listen to what the experts say about a given product and read scientific conclusions of the effects so that you know what you are doing to your body, skin, etc. In this review, I chose an article from Felicia Rose Labs web that demonstrates the most crucial points that you want to know about before using anti aging cream product. In this article, you will know about such products every thing you want and more; you will be an expert. The review will cover the points below thoroughly: 1. Good versus bad vitamin C for skin 2. Types of vitamin C 3. The safest form of vitamin C 4. The most dangerous vitamin C derivative used in skin serums I also attached a picture of the most popular brands of aging cream products based on a lab analysis so that people know what is good/effective/healthy and what's not. ** Note that I am not against using skin care products; I just wanted you to know what are they made of and how/when they can be useful or dangerous. Skin care/anti aging products are important to use because every person starts loosing the collagen during 20s; half of collagen will be lost by 30 years old. Collagen is responsible for keeping the skin smooth. I received this product at a discount or for free in exchange with my honest and unbiased review. =============================================================================================== In this era of profits- over-people, it’s become a health hazard not to closely examine the ingredients found in skin care products. This is particularly true if you’re using an expensive vitamin C serum or cream because the adage “you get what you pay for” tends to make us more trusting than warranted of marketing claims wrapped in fancy packages. While vitamin C is the indisputable champion of anti-aging therapies, most of the vitamin C you’ll find in skin care formulations is a contorted version of the pure active. Many of these derivatives are harmful and found in serums that sell for well over $125 an ounce. Learn about these derivatives to safeguard both face and wallet. *************Good versus bad vitamin C for skin************ If you had to pick just one skin care active to apply for anti-aging benefits, make sure it’s vitamin C. The reasons are well established in the scientific literature and are summarized in the following four points: 1. Vitamin C enables every step of collagen production from stem cell activity to the structural integrity of the skin matrix. 2. Women experience a loss of collagen integrity and production due to fluctuating estrogen levels (Pugliese 2009). 3. Skin levels of vitamin C drop 425% by the time a person reaches middle age (Shindo 1994). 4. The only way to increase skin levels is to apply vitamin C topically (Levine 2001). *********Types of vitamin C********** The following five types of vitamin C are commonly used in cosmetic formulations today. Make a note of their chemical names and check for them on your product’s ingredient list. If you’re not sure about what your ingredient list means,email FeleciaRose or leave a comment and I’ll advise you ASAP. 1. L-ascorbic Acid aka Ascorbic Acid (AA) AA is the water soluble, biologically active form of vitamin C found in nature. This is the form the body uses to build skin, repair wounds, and protect itself from disease and disorder. Be careful of any vitamin C serum that turns from clear to yellow, tan or brown. It contains AA that’s being oxidized by air and light. Some manufacturers color their solutions orange to hide what’s going on. 2. Magnesium Ascorbyl Phosphate (MAP) Magnesium-L-ascorby-Phosphate (VC-PMG) Ascorbic Acid Phosphate (AA2P) These are different names for essentially the same derivative of AA formed by adding magnesium phosphate in a process known as esterification. The addition of the phosphate raises the pH level ascorbic acid remains stable in when in solution. Sodium ascorbyl phosphate is another vitamin C derivative synthesized to deliver the same benefit.Ascorbic acid naturally occurs at a pH of around 3.5 which is fairly acidic. Its acidity creates problems in emulsions. Emulsions are carriers like lotions and creams formulated to make products look and feel nice. The addition of a phosphate group to ascorbic acid, whether magnesium or sodium, raises the pH level it can survive in to greater than 7. 3. Ascorbyl Palmitate aka Ascorbic Acid-6-Palmitate (AA6P) This is another ester of AA using palmitate (palmitic acid) to form an oil-soluble molecule. The idea behind creating an oil-soluble derivative is to enhance penetration through the stratum corneum (SC). The SC contains a large number of lipids (fats) by Nature’s design to help keep out pathogens. Lipid soluble (oil soluble) derivatives are proven to penetrate more readily, however there are major problems with making an AA derivate oil soluble. See our post “Why it can be Disastrous to use the Wrong Vitamin C” for details. In the meantime, if you use a product containing ascorbyl palmitate, be sure to stay out of the sun. Under UV exposure, ascorbyl palmitate is toxic to skin cells and contributes to disease states including skin cancer. 4. Ascorbyl Tretaisopalmitate (ATIP) Tetrahexyldecyl Ascorbate Ascorbyl tretaisopalmitate and tetrahexyldecyl ascorbate are two names for the same molecule. The first (ATIP) is the chemical name while the second (tetrahexyldecyl ascorbate) is the marketing name. It is likely the marketing name was chosen to disassociate it from “palmitate” which as discussed above, is toxic to skin cells under sun exposure. 5. Liposome Vitamin C Encasing a molecule in a liposome is a technique devised by cosmetic chemists to impart stability and penetration properties to AA and other molecules. The molecule is wrapped in a bubble of lipids (the liposome) making it oil soluble which is a really bad idea when it comes to vitamins. Worse, chemists use ascorbyl palmitate when making liposome vitamin C. The addition of more lipids (the liposome) may only worsen the ingredient’s toxicity. Please see our post “Why it can be Disastrous to use the Wrong Vitamin C” for details. *******************The safest form of vitamin C******************* For the naturalists amongst us, it will come as no surprise that the safest form of vitamin C is ascorbic acid – the form found in nature and biologically active in the body. In 1747 a physician working for the British Royal Navy identified vitamin C as a mysterious compound in citrus fruit that cures scurvy. In 1931 a Hungarian scientist isolated the compound and called it hexuronic acid. The name ascorbic acid was later proposed and adopted to acknowledge its anti-scorbutic (scurvy) properties. Through common usage, the term “vitamin C” became a categorical name applied to ascorbic acid and its many derivatives. As a dietary supplement, the base ascorbic acid molecule is modified in a variety of ways to either enhance intestinal absorption or reduce its natural acidity. As a topical skin care ingredient, the base molecule is modified to boost its stability and help it penetrate the top layer of the skin. Whether in the form of a dietary supplement or as an ingredient in a skin serum, the biologically active component of any vitamin C derivative is ascorbic acid. Thus the vitamin C compound must be degraded in the skin or in the body so that free form ascorbic acid is released (Humbert 2003). ****************The most dangerous vitamin C derivative used in skin serums**************** While no one intends to sell dangerous products, recklessness is often the road to ruin. In the world of cosmetics manufacturers, the rush to incorporate vitamin C derivatives into formulas sold as anti-aging serums apparently made safety an ancillary concern. Why investigate and look for trouble? What could go wrong with vitamin C? The poster child for what can go wrong is told in the story of ascorbyl palmitate. Ascorbyl palmitate is a vitamin C derivative formed by adding a fatty acid named palmitic acid to the base ascorbic acid molecule. Fatty acids are building blocks of lipids and palmitic acid is one of the most common. As the name implies, palmitic acid is found in palm trees and coconut oils. ===Palmitic acid is a common fatty acid found in palm tree oils. ++++++++++Lipids and fatty acids are important in skin care because lipids form a major component of the outer layer of the skin. This poses a problem for ascorbic acid because it’s water soluble making it complicated for manufacturers to ensure it passes through the skin’s lipid barrier. An oil soluble derivative was needed and the food industry had already synthesized an oil soluble version to use as a food preservative. Named ascorbyl palmitate, the compound is made by attaching a palmitic acid molecule to an ascorbic acid molecule. One end of the molecule (the AA end) is water soluble and the other end (palmitic acid) is oil soluble. +++++++++A landmark study reported in the Journal of Investigative Dermatology investigated what happens in human skin when ascorbyl palmitate is applied and then exposed to a moderate amount of sunlight – about the same as an average person would be exposed to on a sunny day. The researchers expected ascorbyl palmitate to penetrate the lipid barrier of the skin, but they weren’t sure if it would penetrate the lipid barrier of skin cells. They discovered that it efficiently penetrates both lipid barriers, and that the ascorbic acid very effectively subdued intra-cellular free radical generation. However they were astonished to find out that any gains bought by the ascorbic acid were dramatically outweighed by the pitfalls of the palmitic acid. Their astonishment was apparent in the choice of adjectives they used to describe the havoc. According to the authors, palmitic acid is a lightning rod for UV rays which brought on “catastrophic” skin cell death on a “massive scale.” The authors further warned against using any vitamin C serum with a concentration of ascorbyl palmitate in excess of 100-300 M (micromoles). Distressingly, many cosmetics contain concentrations as high as 15 percent which exceeds the authors’ warning dose by a factor of 1000. The number of cosmetics containing ascorbyl palmitate exceeded 617 in the year 2000, a leap from a year 1992 count of 667 products (Burnnet 2011). Check both your sunscreen and your vitamin C serum for ascorbyl palmitate. The Environmental Working Group is working toward getting the FDA to ban its use in sunscreens. Also check your labels for ascorbyl tretaisopalmitate, tetrahexyldecyl ascorbate and liposome encapsulated vitamin C.

text_full: Great fitbit wristband companion, but somewhat overpriced and not accurate. I bought a fitbit charge hr last week, and I also wanted to buy the companion scale because I used to measure and keep track of my weight on a daily basis. I was also using another device to monitor and track my BMI, so the great think about this scale is that all the information you need is already measured one time, and kept in your fitbit site for you. The main problem (this moves my review from 4 to 3 stars) is that the readings are not accurate. I always weight myself in the morning after I urinated. I did it yesterday 4 times and the four times the weight and the BMI readings were different. Today, I did the same think, I weighted myself two times one right after the other, and the readings were both different. This is disappointing, especially considering the high tag prize. The design is beautiful, setting up was a breeze, and so far everything about this is great. The one feature that goes above and beyond anything I used before is the fact that this scale measure lean vs fat, so you know exactly how many pounds of fat and how many pounds of lean your body contains. This is an essential data to analyze and reconsider what you are eating, so you can really understand the fluctuations in your weight. The reason I am not giving this 5 stars is because this is clearly over prized. The company is kind of taking advantage of the momentum they are having, and I'll go by saying that their products are just excellent. However excellent this is, though, the fair price would be something below $60-$70. it is extremely convenient, though, that by using fitbit products all your data is collected and presented in the same website, so I would highly encourage you to buy this if you have a fitbit band, and if you can afford the high price as I write this review (just below the hundred and twenty). Updated on 4/22: rating down from 4 to 3 stars due to not accurate readings.

text_full: Large, but just okay.. So first off, this is a huge bag. I compared it next to my High Sierra Avenger 45L pack and it is a big difference. Let me first mention the features: • comes with rainfly • has two side pockets on left and right that run the length of the body of the bag • has sleeping bag compartment on the bottom of the back that has a zippable divider • has two walking pole straps • has two compartments in the lid of the bag. The outer one is for the rainfly and has one on the inner • has two left and right net pockets for water bottles • each side has straps for sleeping mat, tent, etc. • has waist strap and sternum strap • front zipper to expose the entire inside of the pack making it easy to get what you need without unstraping the lid So those are the main features. The material is a hex shaped pattern. Kind of like ripstop. It seems like a good enough pattern but does not seem heavy duty. This does make it light weight for this size backpack. But my other 45L pack has the same hex pattern material but is very noticably more heavy duty. The outer lid pocket contains the rain cover but takes up a lot of room. I wish they put a dedicated pocket on the bottom for the rain cover like most other packs. The rain cover in that pocket takes up a lot of room. The inner pocket on the lid is small but good for electronics. The biggest issue I have is the padding on the shoulder and waist straps. They are just too soft. At first glance they are nice big deep padding that looks to create a nice gap of air. But once I put it on with a light load, the padding instantly compresses and the entire back of the pack is on your back which does not allow any air flow. If the padding was stiffer a bit it would be way better. I also wish the waist straps had pockets. I can however strap on some molle pouches on it. I do like the side pockets. At first they seem just like slits with a zipper only big enough to put maps or thin items in. But they do flare so that helps expands it outward. So even if you have your main compartment loaded, you can still stuff things in the side pockets with no problem. The front has a zipper pocket that is very thin. This is good for small electronics or maps. The side straps are great for sleeping mats and my tent. I like this better than other bags that you have to strap those items horizontally on the bottom or top. Overall, this is a decent pack but the main grips are the thin material and the padding. Normally that would knock it down only one star but since this pack is so huge, those two things are crucial. I took this out on two backpacking trips and the padding was just too soft under the load I had which was about 35lbs of gear. For an 80L pack, the weight i had should not have been an issue. But because the padding compressed so fast, it wasn't the most comfortable pack to carry. And when that thin material i can see wearing out after a season. I hope I am wrong about that, but on the last two trips, just putting my pack down on the ground, I was fearing it was gonna rip as well as just the load I had inside it. Now don't get me wrong, this is a good enough pack. I mean it is fully adjustable with the shoulder straps and has straps to adjust the load but compared to just even my budget High Sierra 45L pack, this is subpar.

text_full: Just OK. I have used Norelco shavers for many years and prefer them to all other models I have tried. This review comes from much experience with the brand. This Arcitec design looks fancy and works well, but gets three average stars because it really works no better than the previous non-space-age, less expensive designs. The 1050, 1060, and 1090 all operate the same, they just have a different display: none is better than the other, and don't waste money on the Cleaner accessory. It is fairly comfortable to hold (I prefer the feel of the original model because this is one is smaller), and looks fancy sitting on the counter, but it does not do a better job. It requires cleaning after each use as there is no space for the hairs. I have always cleaned my shavers after each use anyway. Unless you just want the apperance, it is not worth the extra money. Technically: The triple-blade per round head (each cutter has three spinning blade areas) does not do any better than a double cutting blade. Kind of like a Saturday Night Live skit in the 70's, Jim Belushi said, "Buy a triple bladed razor. For those that will believe anything". Lift-and-cut is a ridiculous concept and a marketing ploy, but Norelco's do a nice job. Norelco went back to more diagonal openings with this model, which is good. Many other newer models have lots of little pin-holes which are worthless, as the hairs have no time to enter a small hole with shaving motion. You would have to set it directly on a hair to cut it. The less pin-holes the better. Feel: The head design feels better on the neck, and has not caused razor-burn if I do not stretch the skin tight like I need to with the original model. It takes the same time to shave as my older unit, and I get no better results, no faster. It takes the same time to get a smooth shave, and the same persistance in some areas. Function: It is a little bit easier to shave under the nose, above my mustache, but not a major difference. It is much harder to trim my sideburns with this unit as the heads almost cut my hair on my head above the ears the way it is shaped. Very poorly designed trimmer, so I use my older shaver for that. Battery: Early, new battery life is good, as with most new battery devices. But, it states to not over-charge. Meaning, you need to be around when recharging to unplug it after it is charged; not good for those that shave and must go to work. The other units would shut off after charging. Cleaner/Charger: Again, one needs to be around when it is finished to not over-charge. The cleaner is not necessary and a waste of time, money, and chemicals. I use a razor brush from an older unit, brush it out quickly over the wastebasket (one can't blow it out without getting hair dust all over the bathroom, and it can't be shaken into the wastebasket as easily as the older models), and I spray it quickly with Remington Silicone Lubricant (I can only find it at Wal-Mart, which is the only thing I ever go there for, by the way). Overall: Buy it for looks and keep your old one in the drawer for sideburns. Nicer on the neck. I would return it, BUT, it was a gift, AND I like the look of it. I know, I know!! Update 12-29-07 I purchased a Braun 9595 through J&R on Amazon, and it has a 60 day trial return guarantee. This is the first micro-screen razor I have used and it is better in all respects to the Norelco Arcitec except for the fancy styling. It is fast and comfortable, and my face feels razor smooth. I was able to return the Arcitec and am really happy with this Braun 9595 model.

text_full: Conversational lamp. My interest in the lamp stems from sleep issues, including circadian rhythm. I knew ahead of time that research indicates the amount of light put off by the Per2 lamp isn't likely to have a physical clinical effect. Compare this one with the lumens of their other lamps. But if use of the lamp can help me establish good sleep habits, routine awake/sleep time, then it will be worth the purchase. Let me talk about what the lamp does. My misconception of how it was supposed to work, probably added to my frustration with programming the device. The programming can be tedious as mentioned in other reviews. A video would be great. a) As a desktop lamp, it provides bright, adjustable light for reading. It also includes a digital clock. b) As a dawn simulator, you program what time you want the light to come on. The light turns on and stays on for an hour or so, gradually increasing in brightness. Then it turns off. It doesn't stay on all day with the light automatically adjusting to the time of day. If you want it back on, you turn it on. Adjust it to the brightness level manually or use the autoshift feature discussed next. The dawn activation only has to be activated once. Going forward, it will begin the gradual brightness everyday at whatever time you set. If you get up at the same time every day, less programming.. c) You can have the lamp automatically adjust corresponding to the time of day. No programming is involved, like for the dawn, dusk and alarm settings. Turn the light on, then click a specific button to automatically shift between three discrete stages of light: dawn (5 am - 1 pm), daylight (1 pm - 9 pm), dusk (9 pm - 5 am). These stages are factory set, meaning you can't change them. An easy to use feature, but less flexible. As mentioned above, you can always adjust the brightness up and down manually. d) As an alarm clock, you program the start time just like you do the dawn simulator. If the gradual brightness of the light does not wake you up, you have a fail safe with the alarm. e) As a dusk simulator, you don't set what time the light will go off, you just program the activation. You can then start the dusk simulator any time you want. Once activated, the first click of the power button gradually dims the light off over a 30 minute period, until it is turned completely off. If for some reason, you want to turn the light off right away, press the power button a second time. You only have to activate the dusk simulator once. Going forward, whenever the light is on, the first click of the power button will start the 30 minute power down, the second click an immediate shut off. You can tell when a feature is activated, because its symbol will continually blink. Good. Since I often read and fall asleep with the light on, the dusk simulator with its automatic power off, is the most useful feature. If you are more interested in an adjustable reading lamp, which puts out similar types of light and has an auto shut off option, but not the dusk/dawn timings, I suggest another purchase I made [[ASIN:B00KSQ8ZNA LAMPAT Dimmable LED Desk Lamp, Black]].

text_full: I love this toothbrush, but.... 1. I don't understand these reviews that complain about getting water into the battery compartment and corroding the batteries. I've never had this problem. It would seem that one would have to be really careless for this to happen. Don't submerge it or pour water over it, and you should be fine. 2. Don't worry about battery life. Get some Eneloop rechargeables, and swap them out anywhere from a couple weeks to a couple months and you'll be fine. 3. This does such a good job, my dentist assumes I'm flossing like I'm supposed to be. I'm not. I do use a waterpic, but only a couple times a week these days. My dentist gave me an A+ on my last visit (part of this is because of the fluoride rinse that's been helping strengthen my teeth, but that's another review). So now to the reason I only gave it three stars. I had one of these that we bought years ago. I don't remember how long, but it's been probably 5 years. I'm not exactly sure, but it's been awhile. It's always worked great and still does. We finally got tired of sharing, and when we saw they were only $20 on Amazon we got another one. This second one has had to be replaced under warranty twice in about a year and a half. It just stopped working, both times. No corrosion in the battery compartment or anything. The unit looks pristine, it just stopped working. The first one lasted about 8 months. The second one only about 6 months. So while this is a great product (functionally) and I would still likely buy it again if my current one died out of warranty (can't beat $20) I'm getting concerned about the quality. Here's hoping third time's a charm.

text_full: Awesome logo on a t-shirt that doesn't quite blast off. Look, you can't go wrong with NASA. The world always needs reminders of the program, and of its and science's contributions to society... as they say, "NASA technology is all around you." So, love the logo. Beyond that it gets a little sketchy. The t-shirt, which seems to run true to size, is nice but made of a thinner material than I would have liked... and the logo itself is made of thicker material than I would have liked. I have done some DIY projects with youth in my life that involve transfer of artwork onto a shirt via a hot iron process, and the instructions for preserving the art are a lot like those that come with this shirt. It's a t-shirt you have to wash inside out, you have to wash in cold water, you have to tumble dry on low or hang dry. The logo doesn't feel like part of the shirt, it feels like a thick object in front of the shirt, if that makes any sense. And for $15, when you can get the same type of shirt with the same logo from other manufacturers for $10, well, if I could do it over again I'd skip this one, and maybe even buy it directly from NASA's 'shop' site.

text_full: This product is working. My mother was diagnosed with sarcoidosis about 5 years ago and has been on oxygen since her diagnosis. She's was told by her physicians that she is in Respiratory Failure which causes severe difficulty with breathing. My father was recently diagnosed with Stage 4 lung cancer and after research I decided to purchase Oxy E. My mother has been taking her drops for about 2wks now and states she was feeling a difference on day 2. When my mother was having her good days she would set her oxygen tank on 2 when resting & 6 when active. Her breathing got so bad she could barely walk from one room to the next without gasping for air, she kept her tank on 10. Today she is able to clean house, do dishes and even walk short distances without her oxygen - something she hasn't been able to do for many years since her diagnosis. She is now able to keep her oxygen tank set on 2 even when she's up cleaning and being active. My father stated he did not feel a difference, but I noticed he was breathing better, his eating had increased and he was even talking about adding a bit of exercise to his daily routine. I increased his drops and then his breathing became more difficult and his eating decreased 2 days later. I do not know for certain if it's the cancer or if it's due to the increase in his drops. I took him off the drops, it's been about 4 days now and I started him back today at the lower dosage. I had to research further because the information on the back of the bottle is limited on how to increase. According to my findings I may have increased too soon. I read one can gradually work up to 12 drops 10x's a day depending on severity of condition. I also do not recall the bottle stating add to 80z's of liquid - which is what I also read. Please try this product and if needing to increase dosage amount definitely research online on how to do so. Thanks!

Why is Tamanu oil beneficial and good for skin?: "Common Name: Tamanu Botanical Name: Calophyllum inophyllum Tamanu Calophyllum inophyllum The Dr. Oz Show demonstrating the benefits of Tamanu Oil. Dr. Mehmet Oz is an informed and supportive advocate of the safe use of effective botanical remedies. He allows ample time for the health benefits of these botanicals to be presented in a clear and positive way. The exotic isles of the South Pacific are home to a long-used traditional ingredient which is just now working its way into the US and European topical and cosmetic industries. Since the 1920’s Oil of Tamanu (Calophyllum inophyllum) has been studied in hospitals and by researchers in Europe, Asia and the Pacific islands. The results of this research are impressive. In 1999 and 2000, I travelled to the South Pacific to study the tamanu tree, and the processing of its oil, and delved into its science in earnest. This is what I learned. Tamanu’s Healing Powers Tamanu oil possesses a unique capacity to promote the formation of new tissue, thereby accelerating wound healing and the growth of healthy skin. This process is known as cicatrization. For this reason, it is a widely used traditional topical aid. In Pacific island folk medicine, tamanu oil is applied liberally to cuts, scrapes, burns, insect bites and stings, abrasions, acne and acne scars, psoriasis, diabetic sores, anal fissures, sunburn, dry or scaly skin, blisters, eczema, herpes sores, and to reduce foot and body odor. Tamanu oil is also massaged into the skin to relieve neuralgia, rheumatism and sciatica. Tamanu oil is employed by Polynesian women for promoting healthy, clear, blemish-free skin, and is also used on babies to prevent diaper rash and skin eruptions. Tamanu and Its Dispersal Calophyllum inophyllum is indigenous to Southeast Asia, but is profuse in Polynesia. The tree grows up to 25 or even 30 meters in height, with long, spreading limbs. The tree trunk is typically thick with dark, cracked bark. The tamanu branches are covered with shiny, dark green oval leaves, and small white flowers with yellow centres. The blossoms give off a delightful, sweet perfume. The fruit of the tree, about the size of an apricot, has a thin flesh and a large nut hull inside. Yet the tamanu nut is a botanical oddity. When the fruits of the tree are collected and cracked open, the blond nut kernel inside contains no apparent oil. But when the kernel dries on a rack for a month or so, it turns a deep, chocolate brown, and becomes sticky with a rich, pleasant-smelling oil. Using a simple screw press, the oil is squeezed from the dark kernels. The resulting oil of tamanu is dark green and luxurious. Though oil of tamanu is thick and rich, once it is applied to skin it is readily and completely absorbed, leaving no oily residue. “Tamanu oil possesses a unique capacity to promote the formation of new tissue, thereby accelerating wound healing and the growth of healthy skin. This process is known as cicatrization.” - Chris Kilham Anti-Neuralgic and Skin Healing Activity Traditionally oil of tamanu has enjoyed topical use in Fiji for relieving the pain of sciatica, shingles, neuralgia, rheumatism and leprous neuritis, for which it is effective. In 1918, researchers associated with the French Pharmacopoeia began research into tamanu for topical and subcutaneous use. The French researchers quickly became impressed by tamanu’s cicatrizing properties. In the French medical literature on tamanu oil, several instances of its successful use in cases of severe skin conditions have been reported. In one remarkable instance, a woman was admitted to the St. Louis Hospital in Paris with a large gangrenous ulcer on her leg which would not heal. Though doctors were sure that amputation was inevitable, she was given regular dressings of tamanu oil. The wound healed completely, leaving a smooth, flat scar. In other cases, tamanu oil has been employed successfully to heal severe burns caused by boiling water, chemicals and X-rays. Novel Constituents in Tamanu Oil Oil of tamanu contains three basic classes of lipids, neutral lipids, glycolipids, and phospholipids. The oil also contains a unique fatty acid called calophyllic acid, and a novel antibiotic lactone and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agent called calophyllolide. These and other components of tamanu oil, including anti-inflammatory coumarins, account for some of the oil’s beneficial activity. Based on the known activity of known constituents, it is clear that oil of tamanu possesses antibacterial and anti-inflammatory activities. The unique cicatrizing properties of tamanu oil are not yet explained in existing scientific literature, though this activity is established and accepted. The same is true for tamanu’s anti-neuralgic properties. Tamanu oil is well documented for its relief of neuritis, but the constituents responsible and their modes of activity are not yet known. Product Applications Oil of tamanu is suitable for general skin and cosmetic purposes. The oil’s unusual absorption, its mild and pleasant aroma, and its luxurious feel make it ideal for use in lotions, creams, ointments and other cosmetic products. Considering that tamanu is a potent healing agent with proven benefits, it is only a matter of time before tamanu breaks through to more widespread use, and assumes a position among other successful topical and cosmetic ingredients." text_full: Well-made, stylish wallet. Not the best for carrying cash.. The wallet holds all of my cards, yet is thinner than one or two of my wallets that make me choose which cards to bring. The wallet is not good at holding cash. The cash pocket is sized so close to the width of American currency that each bill has to be gingerly tucked in and aligned. Even with that effort, the wallet cannot fit more than about 3 bills without them crumpling and making the wallet much thicker. If the cash pocket was just 1/4" wider, it would be much more useful for cash. Obviously most transactions today are via credit card or through a smart phone, but there are times when you need to carry cash. Another less significant problem, really more a preference of mine, is that the wallet has a clear plastic ID window. These usually split, get scratched up, and yellow over time. I don't know that I have seen them used more than a handful of times in my entire life. Usually when an ID is required, the person examining it wants to see front and back. This wallet is very good other than for those that frequently carry cash.

text_full: Damaged or do it yourself? Is it cruelty free..... Feathers can be a little controversial. Rest assured that these are cruelty free! I used to have a peacock as a pet. He shed those beautiful tail feathers every year, and even though he is long gone I still have some of his gorgeous plumes. Peacock feathers are not harvested from the animal, you simply pick them up as they are naturally shed. This set arrived in a plastic bag. When I pulled the pieces out, there were three peacock feather pieces and one headband. Each feather piece has a rhinestone accent at the bottom. One is all rhinestone, one is a pearl surrounded by rhinestones, and one is a London blue stone surrounded by rhinestones. Of the two larger pieces, one has an alligator clip hot glued onto the felt backing, and one has a strip of grossgrain ribbon glued to the back. Although I'm not sure, I suspect that it was at one time glued to the headband, or they leave it to the consumer to glue it to the headband. I tried to push the end of the headband through the middle of the ribbon, thinking that perhaps it could slide on, but it is glued completely, you can't slide it onto the headband. The smaller piece also has an alligator type clip of the same size as the larger clipped piece. They stay beautifully in your hair and are actually comfortable. I wouldn't call this a glamor or fashion accessory set, it's definitely a costume set that would be great for a roaring twenties party. Each one would also be a fun addition to a hat. I wear a lot of hats and love to adorn them with scarves and feathers. The following is not part of my review but it is a kind of funny peacock story. naturally, when guests came over they wanted to see him with his tail spread out in beautiful peacock glory. They only open up like that when they're trying to impress someone, and he certainly was never impressed by any of my guests. At the time I also had a miniature pig. That peacock was so in love with the pig that whenever she came near him he would spread out his feathers and shake them hoping she would notice and return his love. Of course that never happened, the pig could care less. But whenever we wanted to show him off to our friends, we would walk the pig over to him and he would immediately open his tail feathers with a great flourish! My friends and I were all impressed. Maggie the pig was not.

text_full: Good gloves for warmth while using a touchscreen; the initial smell does fade.. Even when you live in the south, gloves are a staple of the outdoors in the winter, especially on cold mornings in the car or evening walks. Unfortunately, I often also want to use my phone in those situations, so would end up with a glove on one hand and the other in a pocket in between using it, since the touchscreen would not register any contact from the gloves. These fix that problem, and are stylish gloves to boot. First considerations; these are nice looking black leather gloves. The gloves look stylish, are soft to the touch, and the inner lining is both comfortable and warm. The combination of a leather layer and wool works to keep them lightweight while being reasonably warm. The large size fits my hand well; especially since you will be trying to use a touchscreen through these, you want a snug fit without extra length in the fingers. It has a snap on the wrist, which I don’t use often, but will tighten it up just a bit, whether for look or to keep a little more warmth in. Biggest downside for me was the smell. When I first opened them, it was quite strong, to the point of making me cough. It was like a leather smell, but with a strong chemical overtone. It was still strong enough after a few days that I got a replacement; those had the same issue out of the box. However, after about a week it had diminished enough that I can use them without being overwhelmed; if I bring them to my nose it is still unpleasant, but much less bad. Hopefully in a few weeks that will not be a problem at all - I will update this review at that point. Testing: These work perfectly on my phone, for not super precise actions. I can unlock my phone, make calls, move a map around, start or stop runkeeper, and generally do what I would need to in a car or on a walk. I wouldn’t recommend typing much with these on; the target point is too big to be sure what key you will get. And for those who have a fingerprint scanner to unlock their phone (like my wife) - these will not register as your fingerprint. If you need some warm winter gloves for driving or heading out that will also operate your phone, and your nose isn’t excessively sensitive like mine, these are the gloves for you. Cold wind or bitter sub zero temperatures will cut through them, and they aren’t work gloves. But I like them a lot in spite of the smell, and I expect these to be my regular gloves for several winters to come. The product was provided to me at a discount in exchange for a review. The review is my own.

text_full: Life changing inserts, esp. for high impact exercises and injury-prone feet. I discovered the importance of solid support inserts back in 2007 after my feet could no longer take the injuries sustained by running in minimally arch-supportive shoes with factory soles/inserts. I used the green superfeet (more rigid) brand for several years, then switched to the orange superfeet (more flex) after my arches began to hurt following sustained (6-12 months) high impact exercises (speed rope, weighted jump rope, squat jumps, olympic style weightlifting, cross fit, weight vest training, etc). After blowing out the heels of the plastic part of the orange superfeet twice, I decided to change it up and took a chance with the SOLE Dean Karnazes DK insoles shown here. GREAT DECISION! They form to your feet while providing superior support for the long run. I have had minimal issues with my feet (or knees) since changing, which is saying a hell of a lot for someone as rough on their feet as myself, especially considering I have bunions, med-to-high arches, and bone spurs. I put a different pair of these in my running shoes, hiking boots, gym shoes, and even work shoes. I have had about 4-5 pairs now since about 2010. I can get at least a year out of each pair and that is with a lot of miles. One could probably go much longer than a year with one pair of these inserts, but I try to prevent issues with my gnarly feet these days and regularly changing up inserts and shoes is one approach. Incidentally, I also tried the SOLE thin sport custom for soccer cleats and dress shoes, but found they did not treat my feet as well. Key points: -Don't overheat in the oven! This will ruin the arch support. If anything, pull them out early, they will form over time in your shoe anyhow -If you do heat them, remove from oven and immediately put them in the shoe you plan to use them with, lace up tight and stand in semi-athletic stance for about two minutes (feet shoulder width apart, knees directly over toes, slightly bent) -It's a good idea to put new inserts in new shoes, though they will still work well in shoes you have used for a while - I just like to form them up together, seems to work best -I like to form the inserts to each pair of shoes I have, though I have switched them between various shoes with good success (comfort and support is still maintained) These inserts have been life-changing for me. They allow me to keep doing all the stuff I love without being slowed by injured feet. Worth every cent and then some!

text_full: Better than my flatiron!. I have a graduated bob and bleached (level 12) hair. This means varied lengths, from about 4" to 10", and damaged hair that must be treated very tenderly. Because I favor a smooth underswept style, I was using my flatiron to achieve that look, but first I had to blowdry my hair or my natural wave would still turn through the ironing. A double process is a pain, and the blowdrying takes away the sheen from my hair, making it look lifeless. The brush iron is easy to hold and does not diminish the hair's sheen. I strongly recommend sectioning your hair, doing a little at a time. Don't try to take a large section and roll it...unless you are very precise, it will be easy to cross-roll as you get it out of your hair, creating a nightmare tangle. I take a section and hold the end of the hair so the section goes straight up. Then I put the iron under the hair...the stiff bristles keep the iron awaay from my scalp, so no danger of burning myself (unlike my flatiron). I pull the section of hair down over the iron and keep it like that for about 10 seconds (on 'high', and my hair is fine) then I continuously roll the brush through the hair as I bring it down to the end. I keep rolling it as I let the end curl around and roll it up like a regular curling iron. Because there is no upper grip, there is no danger of getting an indention in the hair. Just beware of cross-rolling the hair. Also, keep your fingers offf the barrel. Easy to say, but I did burn a fingertip. Now I let the cool plastic end of the roller rest in my left palm for guidance, and keep my fingers well awaay. I'll post an update if I have more observations.

text_full: Unflattering - But Truly 100% Cotton. When I was looking to purchase this product, I read many reviews and saw lots of complaints about the fit. I almost didn't purchase them because of those complaints, except for one thing... These were just about the only 100% cotton panties that I was able to find. It turns out that it's very difficult to purchase ladies underclothes in 100% cotton. That was my top priority and because it was a necessity, I rated these 4 stars. They provided what I needed when no one else could. What you should realize is that with all of the spandex, polyester and nylon on the market that help things to fit so great, we are generally spoiled in our expectations regarding how something should fit. We expect panties to fit snugly and not be baggy in places. Unfortunately, if you are in a position where you are purchasing 100% cotton and can't compromise on the fabric blends, you are forced to accept a less flattering fit. So, with that said, all of the reviews about how uncomfortable and unflattering the fit is are true. If you can wear a blend, then I recommend moving on to a different product. However, if you absolutely need 100% cotton, I will say that these work just fine. The colors and designs are not so terrific. That's the actual reason why I downgraded the rating to 4 stars. Of the 12 pairs, 4 that I received were two-toned pink stripes. Ugh. I think I had panties like this when I was six years old. There were a couple pairs of dark red, a couple black (with neon elastic), one grey, two turquoise and a sort of darkish blue. Even the solid colors had elastic in loud accent colors. I hate to think of getting into an accident and being hospitalized with these on. (Shudder.) All opinions expressed in this review are 100% my own. I have shared my personal experience with this product and cannot guarantee that you will have the same experience with the product that I had, nor can I promise that we will share the same opinion of the product.

text_full: Perfect fix for slipping glasses, and much more comfortable than silicone pads!. My eye doctor is unable to make any further adjustments for fit, so they added some adhesive silicone nose pads. These helped with the slipping, but the dents in my skin became worse. I’ve tried 5 different brands of adhesive silicone nose pads (different sizes and thicknesses, butterfly vs. D-shape like these), but I’ve been unable to make my glasses comfortable for the past 2 years. So that’s why I gave these a shot, and so far so good! My plastic frame sunglasses have a similar type of foam pads and I love them, so I’m not sure why I didn’t think to try foam pads sooner! These feel softer and more “squishy,” than the silicone pads I’ve tried, yet they also have a slimmer profile, which means they aren’t nearly as noticeable. The overall size is also perfect for my frames (Cinzia Designs, CIN-5076). The thinner profile seems to do what I need without adding any bulk, and because they are perfectly sized to the nose rest of the frames, they seem to be distributing the weight of my glasses better than the thicker/slightly smaller silicone pads. The edges of the silicone pads would actually dig into my skin, which is really uncomfortable, but these are slim enough that I’m not experiencing that issue. The foam pads are gripping better than the silicone this far, so I think this is the way to go. I’ll update my review if these don’t seem to hold up well, but so far I’m very happy!
